text: The world in which a man lives shapes itself chiefly by the way in which he looks at it, and so it proves different to different men; to one it is barren, dull, and superficial; to another rich, interesting, and full of meaning.
plain: How you see the world decides what it is to you.

text: Health outweighs all other blessings so much that one may really say that a healthy beggar is happier than an ailing king.
plain: Health beats status, money and everything else.

text: An intellectual man in complete solitude has excellent entertainment in his own thoughts and fancies, while no amount of diversity or social pleasure, theatres, excursions and amusements, can ward off boredom from a dullard.
plain: A full mind is never bored alone. An empty one is bored in a crowd.

text: A good, temperate, gentle character can be happy in needy circumstances, whilst a covetous, envious and malicious man, even if he be the richest in the world, goes miserable.
plain: Character makes you happy broke. Greed makes you miserable rich.

text: In plain language, every man is pent up within the limits of his own consciousness, and cannot directly get beyond those limits any more than he can get beyond his own skin; so external aid is not of much use to him.
plain: You live inside your own head, and nobody can fix that from outside.

text: All the pride and pleasure of the world, mirrored in the dull consciousness of a fool, are poor indeed compared with the imagination of Cervantes writing his Don Quixote in a miserable prison.
plain: A great mind in a cell beats a fool with everything.

text: In general, indeed, the wise in all ages have always said the same thing, and the fools, who at all times form the immense majority, have in their way too acted alike, and done just the opposite; and so it will continue.
plain: Everyone knows what is wise. Almost nobody does it.

text: It is not what things are objectively and in themselves, but what they are for us, in our way of looking at them, that makes us happy or the reverse.
plain: It is not the event that hurts you, it is how you look at it.

text: The man who is cheerful and merry has always a good reason for being so,--the fact, namely, that he is so.
plain: Being cheerful is its own reason.

text: So if cheerfulness knocks at our door, we should throw it wide open, for it never comes inopportunely; instead of that, we often make scruples about letting it in.
plain: Let joy in when it shows up. Do not wait for permission.

text: Even trees must be shaken by the wind, if they are to thrive.
plain: You need resistance to grow.

text: It follows from all this that the greatest of follies is to sacrifice health for any other kind of happiness, whatever it may be, for gain, advancement, learning or fame, let alone, then, for fleeting sensual pleasures.
plain: Never trade your health for money, fame or fun.

text: The most general survey shows us that the two foes of human happiness are pain and boredom.
plain: Life swings between pain and boredom.

text: Nothing is so good a protection against such misery as inward wealth, the wealth of the mind, because the greater it grows, the less room it leaves for boredom.
plain: Build your mind and boredom has nowhere to live.

text: True, if quality of intellect could be made up for by quantity, it might be worth while to live even in the great world; but unfortunately, a hundred fools together will not make one wise man.
plain: Crowds do not add up to wisdom.

text: Ordinary people think merely how they shall spend their time; a man of any talent tries to use it.
plain: Ordinary people kill time. Talented people use it.

text: Because people have no thoughts to deal in, they deal cards, and try and win one another's money.
plain: People with nothing in their heads fill the hours with games.

text: What one human being can be to another is not a very great deal: in the end every one stands alone, and the important thing is who it is that stands alone.
plain: In the end you stand alone, so what matters is who you are.

text: There is not much to be got anywhere in the world. It is filled with misery and pain; and if a man escapes these, boredom lies in wait for him at every corner.
plain: The world hands you pain, and if not pain then boredom.

text: In such a world as this, a man who is rich in himself is like a bright, warm, happy room at Christmastide, while without are the frost and snow of a December night.
plain: If you are rich inside, the cold outside does not reach you.

text: Nay more; it is evil which generally has the upper hand, and folly makes the most noise.
plain: Evil usually wins and fools are loud. Do not take either as proof of anything.

text: It is a great piece of folly to sacrifice the inner for the outer man, to give the whole or the greater part of one's quiet, leisure and independence for splendor, rank, pomp, titles and honor.
plain: Do not sell your peace and independence for status.

text: Card-playing is, in fact, a mere tickling of the will.
plain: Games are cheap stimulation for a bored mind.

text: The ordinary life of every day, so far as it is not moved by passion, is tedious and insipid; and if it is so moved, it soon becomes painful.
plain: Ordinary life is dull until passion shows up, then it hurts.

text: The ordinary man places his life's happiness in things external to him, in property, rank, wife and children, friends, society, and the like, so that when he loses them or finds them disappointing, the foundation of his happiness is destroyed.
plain: Put your happiness in outside things and they can wreck it.

text: The man of inner wealth wants nothing from outside but the negative gift of undisturbed leisure, to develop and mature his intellectual faculties, that is, to enjoy his wealth; in short, he wants permission to be himself, his whole life long, every day and every hour.
plain: What you need is room to be yourself.

text: The great affliction of all philistines is that they have no interest in ideas, and that, to escape being bored, they are in constant need of realities.
plain: Shallow people need constant action because ideas bore them.

text: In much wisdom is much grief; and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.
plain: The more you know, the more it hurts.

text: Riches, one may say, are like sea-water; the more you drink the thirstier you become; and the same is true of fame.
plain: Wealth and fame make you thirstier, not satisfied.

text: A man never feels the loss of things which it never occurs to him to ask for; he is just as happy without them; whilst another, who may have a hundred times as much, feels miserable because he has not got the one thing he wants.
plain: You are only as poor as the things you want and lack.

text: Discontent springs from a constant endeavor to increase the amount of our claims, when we are powerless to increase the amount which will satisfy them.
plain: You get unhappy when your wants grow faster than your means.

text: Money alone is absolutely good, because it is not only a concrete satisfaction of one need in particular; it is an abstract satisfaction of all.
plain: Money is the one good that stands in for every other.

text: Countless numbers of people find themselves in want, simply because, when they had money, they spent it only to get momentary relief from the feeling of boredom which oppressed them.
plain: People go broke spending to escape boredom.

text: If you stroke a cat, it will purr; and, as inevitably, if you praise a man, a sweet expression of delight will appear on his face; and even though the praise is a palpable lie, it will be welcome, if the matter is one on which he prides himself.
plain: Flattery works on everyone, even when it is false.

text: It is solicitude about what others will say that underlies all our vanity and pretension, yes, and all our show and swagger too.
plain: Most vanity and show is fear of what people will say.

text: And if ever we have had an opportunity of seeing how the greatest of men will meet with nothing but slight from half-a-dozen blockheads, we shall understand that to lay great value upon what other people say is to pay them too much honor.
plain: Even great people get dismissed by fools. Their opinion is not worth your weight.

text: It is observable that a retired mode of life has an exceedingly beneficial influence on our peace of mind, and this is mainly because we thus escape having to live constantly in the sight of others, and pay everlasting regard to their casual opinions; in a word, we are able to return upon ourselves.
plain: Less time in other people's eyes means more peace.

text: Pride works from within; it is the direct appreciation of oneself. Vanity is the desire to arrive at this appreciation indirectly, from without.
plain: Pride comes from inside. Vanity begs for it from outside.

text: The cheapest sort of pride is national pride; for if a man is proud of his own nation, it argues that he has no qualities of his own of which he can be proud; otherwise he would not have recourse to those which he shares with so many millions of his fellowmen.
plain: Being proud of what millions share means you have nothing of your own.

text: No doubt, when modesty was made a virtue, it was a very advantageous thing for the fools; for everybody is expected to speak of himself as if he were one.
plain: Modesty is a gift to fools, who then pretend to be equals.

text: Every nation mocks at other nations, and all are right.
plain: Everybody is a fool to somebody, and they are right.

text: The man who breaks confidence has for ever forfeited confidence, whatever he may do, and whoever he may be; and the bitter consequences of the loss of confidence can never be averted.
plain: Break trust once and you are done.

text: Do you think, said Socrates, that if an ass happened to kick me, I should resent it?
plain: Socrates would not resent a kick from a donkey, so why resent a fool?

text: True appreciation of his own value will make a man really indifferent to insult; but if he cannot help resenting it, a little shrewdness and culture will enable him to save appearances and dissemble his anger.
plain: If you know your worth, insults slide off.

text: A man must himself have but a poor opinion of his own worth who hastens to prevent the utterance of an unfavorable opinion by giving his enemy a black eye.
plain: Hitting back shows you doubt your own worth.

text: Fame is the undying brother of ephemeral honor.
plain: Fame outlives honor.

text: Everyone can make a claim to honor; very few to fame, as being attainable only in virtue of extraordinary achievements.
plain: Anyone can have honor. Fame takes extraordinary work.

text: The influence of an action, be it never so noble, can last but a short time; but a work of genius is a living influence, beneficial and ennobling throughout the ages.
plain: Deeds fade. Great work keeps working for centuries.

text: Of Alexander the Great we have but the name and the record; but Plato and Aristotle, Homer and Horace are alive, and as directly at work to-day as they were in their own lifetime.
plain: Alexander is a name. Plato and Homer are still at work.

text: That was an incomparable fine saying of Seneca's, that fame follows merit as surely as the body casts a shadow; sometimes falling in front, and sometimes behind.
plain: Merit gets recognized, sometimes late.

text: As a general rule, the longer a man's fame is likely to last, the later it will be in coming; for all excellent products require time for their development.
plain: The longer the fame will last, the later it arrives.

text: The fame which lasts to posterity is like an oak, of very slow growth; and that which endures but a little while, like plants which spring up in a year and then die; whilst false fame is like a fungus, shooting up in a night and perishing as soon.
plain: Lasting fame grows like an oak. Fake fame pops up like a mushroom and dies.

text: People are more likely to appreciate the man who serves the circumstances of his own brief hour, or the temper of the moment,--belonging to it, living and dying with it.
plain: Easy to love the man of the moment. He dies with the moment.

text: There is but one thing to be done, though how difficult!--the foolish must become wise,--and that they can never be.
plain: The only fix for fools is wisdom, and they never get it.

text: The man who seeks to do what is good and genuine, must avoid what is bad, and be ready to defy the opinions of the mob, nay, even to despise it and its misleaders.
plain: Do good work, and be ready to ignore the crowd.

text: The truth is that fame means nothing but what a man is in comparison with others.
plain: Fame is only comparison.

text: Not fame, but that which deserves to be famous, is what a man should hold in esteem.
plain: Respect what deserves fame, not the fame itself.

text: It would be a miserable existence which should make its value or want of value depend upon what other people think; but such would be the life of a hero or a genius if its worth consisted in fame, that is, in the applause of the world.
plain: If your worth depends on other people, your life is miserable.

text: He who deserves fame without getting it possesses by far the more important element of happiness, which should console him for the loss of the other.
plain: If you earned it but did not get it, you still hold what matters.

text: If admiration were his chief aim, there would be nothing in him to admire.
plain: If you only want admiration, there is nothing in you to admire.

text: The truest fame, the fame that comes after death, is never heard of by its recipient; and yet he is called a happy man.
plain: The best fame arrives after you are gone, and you are happy anyway.

text: It is only work done from the heart that ever gains the laurel.
plain: Only work you mean ever wins anything.

text: The value of posthumous fame lies in deserving it; and this is its own reward.
plain: Deserving it is the reward.

text: People are always swayed by authority; and where fame is widespread, it means that ninety-nine out of a hundred take it on faith alone.
plain: Most fame is people repeating what they were told.

text: Would a musician feel flattered by the loud applause of an audience if he knew that they were nearly all deaf, and that, to conceal their infirmity, they set to work to clap vigorously as soon as ever they saw one or two persons applauding?
plain: Applause means nothing if the crowd cannot tell good from bad.

text: Life is such a poor business that the strictest economy must be exercised in its good things.
plain: Life is thin, so spend its good things carefully.

text: There is no greater consolation in age than the feeling of having put the whole force of one's youth into works which still remain young.
plain: Put your whole youth into work that stays young.
